card.problem_text:
Cook's membrane (2D linear elasticity, compressible and nearly incompressible), SWG/weak Galerkin scheme on polygonal meshes.
Geometry: Tapered plate (classical Cook's membrane), 2D. The text gives dimensions only through Figure 10.4. The one coordinate stated is the midpoint of the right end, Q = (48, 52). The full vertex coordinates are not given in the text.
Material: Linear isotropic elasticity, not hyperelastic. Case 1: E = 1, ν = 1/3. Case 2 (nearly incompressible): E = 1.12499998125, ν = 0.499999975. The section does not say whether this is plane strain or plane stress.
Boundary conditions: One end (the left end) is clamped. A shear traction is applied on the opposite end. The remaining edges are presumably traction-free, but the text does not say so explicitly.
Loading: Shear traction g = (0, 1/16) applied on the end opposite the clamp (the right end). The section does not say whether this is a distributed traction or a total force.
Discretisation in the paper: Reference solution: taken from literature values in [2, 22]. Their mesh, element type and element count are not stated. (The SWG computations under test used triangle, quadrilateral, hexagonal and octagonal partitions, with h = 1/16 in the figures. For example, the triangular mesh had 8,192 elements and 12,416 DOF at the fifth refinement. These describe the tested method, not the reference.)
Features: Corners where the clamped left edge meets the traction-free top and bottom edges. Linear elasticity has a stress singularity here; for near-incompressibility the pressure is also singular. Peak stress or pressure at these corners will not converge under refinement.; Corners where the loaded right edge meets the free top and bottom edges. Uniform traction meets a free edge at a convex corner, giving a stress concentration that may be weak, not a strong singularity. The section does not discuss it..
Question: which of these quantities can serve as trustworthy reference values: Vertical displacement at Q vs. total DOF (convergence curve) (How the tip displacement at Q changes with the number of DOF, for triangle, quadrilateral, hexagonal and octagonal partitions, case 2); Deformation, pseudo-pressure and displacement contour fields (Qualitative contour plots of the deformation coloured by pseudo-pressure, and of u1 and u2, for κ = 1 and κ = 0, h = 1/16)?

spec.name: Cook's membrane: 2D linear elasticity, compressible and nearly incompressible, SWG (weak Galerkin) on polygonal meshes
spec.geometry: The classical Cook's membrane: a tapered quadrilateral plate in 2D. The text defines it only through Figure 10.4. The one stated coordinate is Q = (48, 52), the midpoint of the right (loaded) end. The full vertex coordinates are not given in the text. The classical Cook's geometry would place Q at that point, but it has to be confirmed from the figure before it is used.
spec.material:
Linear isotropic elasticity, not hyperelastic, so this is outside the pipeline's usual hyperelastic scope.
- Case 1 (compressible): E = 1, ν = 1/3.
- Case 2 (nearly incompressible): E = 1.12499998125, ν = 0.499999975.
The two parameter sets appear chosen to give the same shear modulus, with the bulk/Lamé modulus becoming very large in case 2. The section does not say whether this is plane strain or plane stress. The figure parameter κ (κ = 1 and κ = 0) is not defined in the text given.
spec.loading: A shear traction g = (0, 1/16) is applied on the right end, opposite the clamped left end. It is not stated whether g is a distributed traction (force per unit length) or a total resultant force. The top and bottom edges are presumably traction-free, but this is not stated explicitly. Because the problem is linear elasticity, there are no limit points or load-level effects.
qois: Vertical displacement u2 at Q = (48, 52) plotted against total DOF (convergence curve), for triangle, quadrilateral, hexagonal and octagonal partitions, case 2 (nearly incompressible). This is a candidate trustworthy reference QoI: it is a point displacement away from the singular corners, and displacements converge under refinement even with the clamped-free corner singularities, provided the scheme is free of locking.

Deformation contours coloured by pseudo-pressure, and u1 and u2 contour fields, for κ = 1 and κ = 0 at h = 1/16. These are qualitative plots only and are not trustworthy reference values. The u1 and u2 fields are smooth enough to compare visually. The pseudo-pressure is singular at the clamped corners in the nearly incompressible case, so its peak values (and the colour-scale extremes) will not converge under refinement.
well_posedness: The clamped left edge removes rigid-body motions, so the linear elasticity problem has a unique solution as long as the remaining edges are traction-free (presumed, not stated).

Material stability: case 1 (ν = 1/3) is clearly elliptic. Case 2 (ν → 0.5) stays well-posed but approaches the incompressible limit, so convergence that holds uniformly in ν needs a locking-free discretisation. Locking would make the tip displacement converge slowly or to the wrong value at practical DOF counts.

Plane strain versus plane stress decides whether ν = 0.499999975 actually produces near-incompressibility. In plane stress the effective in-plane bulk modulus stays bounded and the problem is not nearly incompressible. This must be resolved before case 2 can be interpreted.
Load level: the problem is linear, so there are no limit points, bifurcation or load-step dependence. Displacements scale linearly with g.

Singular features: where the clamped left edge meets the free top and bottom edges, the stresses are singular. In case 2 the pressure is also singular. Peak stress and pressure there will not converge, and stress or pressure convergence in L2 is degraded. Energy, displacements (including u2 at Q) and region averages away from the corners still converge.

The convex corners where the loaded right edge meets the free edges carry a uniform traction against a free edge, which can produce a weak stress concentration. Pointwise stress near these corners should be treated cautiously. Displacement at Q (the edge midpoint) is not directly affected.
Reference value: it is taken from the literature [2, 22] with no stated mesh, element or DOF count, so its own discretisation error cannot be assessed from this text.
open_questions: What are the full vertex coordinates of the membrane? Only Q = (48, 52) is given in the text; confirm against Figure 10.4.
Is the problem plane strain or plane stress? This decides whether case 2 is actually nearly incompressible.
Is g = (0, 1/16) a distributed traction per unit length or a total shear force on the right edge?
Are the top and bottom edges traction-free? This is presumed but not stated.
What does κ mean in the contour figures (κ = 1, κ = 0)? It is not defined in the provided text. Is it a scheme or stabilisation parameter, a Kolosov-type constant, or a case label?

What is the reference value for u2 at Q in [2, 22], and what mesh, element type and DOF count was it obtained with? Without this, how large the reference error is relative to the SWG error cannot be judged.

Element enum mismatch: the tested SWG/weak Galerkin method uses triangle, quadrilateral, hexagonal and octagonal polygonal partitions, and none of these fits the allowed element list. Q4 was picked only as a placeholder. The method's polynomial degree and its expected convergence order are not stated.

Reference enum mismatch: the actual reference is a set of literature values. 'mesh_refinement_family' was chosen on the assumption that those values are converged fine-mesh results. Is that assumption correct?
The material is linear elastic, not hyperelastic. Confirm that this problem is in scope for the hyperelasticity verification pipeline.

Are the h = 1/16 contour plots meant only as qualitative evidence? If any quantitative contour values (for example pressure extremes) are claimed, they are not trustworthy because of the corner singularities.

sources.quote: Cook's membrane (2D linear elasticity, compressible and nearly incompressible)
Shear traction g = (0, 1/16) applied on the end opposite the clamp (the right end)
One end (the left end) is clamped.

assumptions: I modelled Case 1 (E = 1, nu = 1/3). Case 2 has nu = 0.499999975, which is above the pipeline limit of 0.49, so I could not model it. The DOF convergence curve the user asked about is for case 2, so this model can only check the setup in the compressible regime. It does not check the case 2 values.

The text does not give the vertex coordinates (they are only in Figure 10.4), so I used the standard Cook's membrane geometry [[0,0],[48,44],[48,60],[0,44]]. This matches the stated Q = (48, 52), the midpoint of the right end.

The section does not say whether it is plane strain or plane stress. I chose plane strain because that is the usual setting for the near-incompressibility version of Cook's membrane. Under the other choice the displacement values would differ.
I took g = (0, 1/16) as a uniform distributed traction per unit length on the right edge (length 16), so the total vertical force is 1. The text does not say whether g is a traction or a total force.
I assumed the top and bottom edges are traction-free. The text only says this is 'presumably' so.

Trustworthiness: the vertical displacement at Q is a global, smooth quantity. It should converge under refinement even with the singularities at the clamped corners, so it can serve as a reference value. The literature reference values [2, 22] were not checked here, and the case 2 curve is not covered by this model. The contour fields (deformation, pseudo-pressure, u1, u2) are only qualitative. Near the clamped corners the pseudo-pressure is singular and its peak values will not converge, so they cannot serve as quantitative reference values.
